items.title: 17.2 Relation Between Mean Power and Maximum Power for an Alternating Current

source_refs.note: Topic 17.2 as printed with Example 17.2 and the boxes (PDF 89-90, printed 85-86); Fig 17.4 redrawn.

blocks.text: An alternating current is a current that periodically reverses direction, causing the voltage and current to fluctuate sinusoidally. A resistive load is one that does not store energy (like a capacitor or inductor) and simply dissipates energy as heat.

blocks.title: Instantaneous power
blocks.text: The instantaneous power P in a circuit is the power at any given moment in time t.

where V is the instantaneous voltage and I is the instantaneous current. The maximum or peak Pₘₐₓ occurs when the current and voltage are at their peak values, Iₒ and Vₒ respectively. Also the mean power Pₘₑₐₙ is the average power over one complete cycle of the AC waveform as shown in Fig.17.4.

blocks.alt: A graph of power P against time: an orange curve rises from zero to the dashed line VoIo, labelled maximum power and peak value, falls back to zero and repeats, never going below zero. A second dashed line at (1/2) VoIo is labelled mean power.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.4: Mean power is exactly half the maximum power (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 17.4 also points a 'Peak voltage' arrow at VoIo. VoIo is the peak power, not a voltage, so that label is left out above.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints IR²ᵣₘₛ here; from Eq. 17.7 it is I²ᵣₘₛR = Pₘₑₐₙ (the square is on the current, not on R).

Therefore, it can be concluded that the mean power in a resistive load is half the maximum power for a sinusoidal alternating current or voltage because the instantaneous power in an AC circuit varies over time. While the instantaneous power reaches at maximum value at certain points in the cycle, it spends significant time at zero or lower values, resulting in an average power that is half the peak value.

blocks.title: Example 17.2
blocks.problem: An alternating voltage supplied across a resistor of 50 Ω has a voltage of 220 V. Calculate the mean power in kilo watt of the system.
steps:
Putting the values
Pₘₐₓ = (220 V)²/50 Ω = 968 W

As the mean power is half of the maximum (peak) power,
Pₘₑₐₙ = Pₘₐₓ/2 = 968 W/2
